"Write whatever comes to you." It is a strange instruction, because the moment you tell yourself to write whatever comes, your mind goes blank. You begin to notice the noise of the refrigerator, the hum of a laptop, the distant siren. Writing feels like trying to catch smoke with a fork. But then a single phrase surfaces: the smell of rain on hot pavement. You hold onto it. You start there.

Rain on hot pavement: wet dust, almost metallic. I remember standing on a sidewalk in late July. Clouds had gathered above the oaks, sudden and gray. Then the first heavy drops, each one exploding into a tiny puff of steam. There is no smell quite like that, except maybe the smell of a turned-up garden after a storm, or the chlorine and sunscreen and cookout smoke that clings to a summer evening. Memory attaches itself to smells more stubbornly than to pictures. A certain aftershave and I am six years old, hugging my grandfather. A whiff of cinnamon and I am in a kitchen where someone is rolling dough for apple pies. The brain is an archive of invisible files, and the nose owns the key.

I have been thinking about time, too. It passes like a river, but not in a straight line. Some moments stay in place because of their weight—a hospital hallway, a first kiss, the sound of a key in the door after months apart. Others dissolve instantly. Yesterday I could not remember what I ate for lunch. Yet on the playground in my mind, the exact pattern of cracks in the asphalt is still visible, and the feel of the metal slide in July is still hot. Memory is not a timeline. It is more like a garden: plants grow where seeds happened to fall, and some seeds are tiny but stubborn.

Maybe that's why writing feels natural. It is an attempt to organize the garden, to decide what to keep and what to let go. When you write, you are not merely storing words. You are choosing which moments are real in the only way that matters. There is a story about a man who lost his memory and wrote everything in a notebook. He wrote the names of his children, the location of his house, the fact that he liked coffee but not tea. When the notebook was stolen, he lost himself entirely. We are all living inside our own notebooks, though most of us never see the pages.

The present is a strange country. We live in it, but we are usually somewhere else. I am typing this and half-wondering if there is cheese in the refrigerator, whether the car needs gas, what time the pharmacy closes. Meanwhile the cursor blinks steadily, patient as a heartbeat. The mind is a pack of untrained dogs, and the only trick is to make them sit for a little while. Focus is not a natural state. It is a craft. It is the art of returning, again and again, to the same point, like a sailor tacking against the wind. When I am asked to write whatever comes to me, I am really being asked to let the dogs run. But even the dogs need a fence, or they will chase every squirrel of thought until nightfall. The fence here is the page. The leash is the sentence.

I think about the people I have met. The cashier who smiled as if she had a secret. The man on the bus who sang softly to himself, a tune I almost recognized. The woman in the hospital waiting room who offered me a piece of gum from a crumpled pack. We are surrounded by strangers whose inner lives are as complex as our own, yet we will never know them. A novelist can spend a whole book inside one character and still not exhaust that person. How much more mysterious is the real person, who cannot be contained by any book. We are each a universe with a skin around it. And somehow, in this vast scattering of universes, we collide, exchange a few particles of kindness, and continue on our trajectories.

There is a kind of faith in writing. You cannot see the finished piece at the beginning. You can only see the next word, the next sentence. It is like walking through a forest at night with a small flashlight: the beam shows only a few feet ahead, but each step reveals the next. Sometimes the path turns out to be a circle. Sometimes it leads you to a clearing you did not know you were looking for. The first draft is not the destination. It is only the act of putting one foot in front of the other, trusting that the ground will hold. There is a special courage in the blank page. It stares back with infinite whiteness, and it does not care about your fear. But it rewards persistence. The blank page is an enemy of none who are willing to write badly at first.

I used to think that inspiration was something that arrived from nowhere, like lightning. Later I learned that it is more like a small animal: it comes when you are quiet, when you have made a comfortable place for it. It rarely comes when you shout for it. It comes in the shower, on a walk, at 3 a.m., after you have already given up. The best ideas are often the ones that seem to have been waiting under the floorboards, listening to you work. You sit down, you write, you delete, you rewrite. Then one day a sentence appears that feels almost alive. You do not know where it came from. It was not in the thoughts you planned. It was under the floorboards all along.

The beginning was about rain and memory. The middle became a meditation on attention and strangers. The end may bring us back to the beginning, because true circles are always returning. That is the power of words: they do not describe the world; they build another one alongside it. A thousand words is a small city. In this city, we have walked down wet sidewalks, smelled summer, met strangers, lost and found ourselves. There is no need for a moral. There is no need for a plot. The only requirement is that we keep moving, one sentence at a time, and let the next word come of its own free will.
